metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Loving v. United States

Opinion filed: 1996-06-10

Docket No.: 94-1966

Citations:
• 135 L. Ed. 2d 36
• 116 S. Ct. 1737
• 517 U.S. 748
• 1996 U.S. LEXIS 3593

Case holding summaries:
• discussing history of the expansion of court-martial jurisdiction and stating "[o]ver the next two centuries, Congress expanded court-martial jurisdiction"
• stating that "it remains a basic principle of our constitutional scheme that one branch of the [g]overnment may not intrude upon the central prerogatives of another"
• "[T]he lawmaking function belongs to Congress ... and may not be conveyed to another branch or entity"
• "Though in 1935 we struck down two delegations for lack of an intelligible principle, A.L.A. Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States, 295 U.S. 495, 55 S.Ct. 837, 79 L.Ed. 1570 (1935
• "Though in 1935 we struck down two delegations for lack of an intelligible principle, A.L.A. Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States, 295 U.S. 495, 55 S.Ct. 837, 79 L.Ed. 1570 (1935), and Panama Refining Co. v. Ryan, 293 U.S. 388, 55 S.Ct. 241, 79 L.Ed. 446 (1935
• noting that the Supreme Court gives Congress "the highest deference" in ordering military affairs
• "Even when a branch does not arrogate power to itself, moreover, the separation-of-powers doctrine requires that a branch not impair another in the performance of its constitutional duties." (citing Mistretta v. United States, 488 U.S. 361, 397-408 (1989)
• "subsequent legislation declaring the intent of an earlier statute is entitled to great weight in statutory construction"
• "Even when a branch does not arrogate power to itself, moreover, the separation-of-powers doctrine requires that a branch not impair another in the performance of its constitutional duties." (citing Mistretta v. United States, 488 U.S. 361, 397-408 (1989)
• stating that the “President, acting in his constitutional office of Commander in Chief, had undoubted competency to prescribe” R.C.M. provisions
• "The fundamental precept of the delegation doctrine is that the lawmaking function belongs to Congress, U.S. Const., Art. I, S 1, and may not be conveyed to another branch or entity."
• "Though in 1935 we struck down two delegations for lack of an intelligible principle, we have since upheld without exception, delegations under standards phrased in sweeping terms."
• when delegated duty is interlinked with duties already assigned to President by Constitution, the same limitations on legislative delegation do not apply as when power is granted solely by delegation
• legislation declaring the intent of an earlier statute is entitled to great weight in statutory construction
• noting that "[e]ven before the birth of this country, separation of powers was known to be a defense against tyranny"
• Congress may not remove executive officers except by impeachment
• upholding delegation to the Federal Communications Commission to regulate radio broadcasting according to "public interest, convenience, or necessity"
• general rule is that "[a] constitutional power implies a power of delegation of authority under it sufficient to effect its purposes"
• "The responsibility for determining how best our Armed Forces shall attend to th[e] business [of fighting or preparing to fight wars] rests with Congress and with the President"
• Congress may not deprive court of jurisdiction based on the outcome of a case or undo a Presidential pardon
• examining whether law requiring agency control of Presidential papers disrupted the functioning of the Executive
• President has inherent authority to convene courts-martial
• analyzing court-martial punishments under the Eighth Amendment
• recognizing "the necessity of adapting legislation to complex conditions involving a host of details with which the national legislature cannot deal directly"
• explaining that delegations calling "for the exercise of judgment or discretion that lies beyond the traditional authority of the President" are more likely to violate the separation of powers
• determining that courts-martial only had jurisdiction of serviceconnected crimes
• discussing a provision in the British Articles of War of 1774 providing court-martial jurisdiction of civilian offenses by soldiers
• "The power of the executive to establish rules and regulations for the government of the army, is undoubted"
• Congress may not revise judicial determinations by retroactive legislation reopening judgments
• overruling O'Callahan and taking issue with its historical analysis
• Congress may not enact laws without bicameral passage and presentment of the bill to the President
• "The fundamental precept of the delegation doctrine is that the lawmaking function belongs to Congress, U.S. Const., Art. I, § 1, and may not be conveyed to another branch or entity."
• recognizing that Congress has delegated to the President the authority to address modes of proof and punishment that a court-martial may direct
• noting that the usual “limitations on delegation [of congressional powers] 3 America’s military response began before the attacks of September 11th had been completed. See The 9/11 Commission Report 20 (2004
• "subsequent legislation declaring the intent of an earlier statute is entitled to great weight in statutory construction"
• acknowledging that Congress “may not delegate the power to make laws”
• explaining that the dele- gation doctrine is less restrictive in such circumstances, cit- ing United States v. Mazurie, 419 U.S. 544, 556–57 (1975), and United States v. Curtiss-Wright Export Corp., 299 U.S. 304, 319–22 (1936)
• "This Court established long ago that Congress must be permitted to delegate to others at least some authority that it could exercise itself"
• finding that Congress delegated to the Presi- dent the authority to designate death penalty aggravating factors
• "Even when a branch does not arrogate power to itself, moreover, the separation- of-powers doctrine requires that a branch not impair another in the performance of its constitutional duties."
• “Even before the birth of this country, separation of powers was known to be a defense against tyranny.”
• "[e]ven when a branch does not arrogate power to itself, ... the separation-of-powers doctrine requires that a branch not impair another in the performance of its constitutional duties"
